Dear Ayesha,
I owe you an apology for yesterday's chemistry "help."
You asked me how to balance that equation, and I rattled off, "Just count the atoms, fix the coefficients, don't touch the subscripts, easy." Then I did three examples in about two minutes. You kept nodding, so I thought you had it.
Today in the test I saw you sitting with your pen still for ten minutes on question four. That's when I understood. You were nodding because I was going so fast you didn't know what to ask.
I forgot that a month ago I didn't know what a coefficient was either. I learned it slowly, from Ma'am, with drawings.
So can we try again on Saturday? This time you do the example, I only ask questions, and if I say a word you don't know, you stop me. I promise not to say "easy."
Your friend,
Jahnavi

qa.a: Question four.

So, Mehta ma'am asked me to talk about peer tutoring for the school podcast. I'm Sachin, Class Eleven, and here's my big failure.
My friend Wasim missed two weeks with a fever, and I offered to catch him up on coding. I opened my laptop and went, "Okay, so you just loop through the array, increment the counter, break when you hit the condition." Twenty minutes, very fast, lots of words from class. Wasim kept saying, "Yeah, yeah, okay."
Next day's practical, he couldn't write a single loop. He told me later he didn't know what "array" meant. He hadn't wanted to look slow.
Honestly, I felt terrible. And a little annoyed, because he said yes. But then I remembered I had nodded exactly like that in Class Nine.
Second time, I drew boxes on paper. Each box a locker. No words he didn't know. He wrote his first loop in ten minutes.

qa.a: Wasim missed two weeks with a fever.

Dear Mrs Fernandes,
You once told our class that the best way to learn physics was to teach it. I thought that was something teachers say. This term I found out you were right.
I'm tutoring a first-year student, Omkar, twice a week. In the first session he asked why a heavier ball and a lighter ball fall at the same speed. I started to answer and realised I only knew the rule, not the reason. I said, "Let me come back to you." My face was hot the whole way home.
I spent that weekend with my old notes and the textbook, working it through until I could say it simply. Next session I explained it with two bottles, one full and one empty. Omkar got it, and so, honestly, did I.
Every week he finds another hole in what I thought I knew. It is humbling and oddly fun.
With thanks,
Bhavna

Chinmay, you're scared to ask your seniors things? Let your Samir uncle tell you about my first year at the tool factory.
They put me under a machinist called Bhosale. Brilliant hands. But every time I asked a question, he sighed like I had insulted him. "I already told you. Are you slow?" After the third sigh I stopped asking. I nodded. I said, "Yes, got it," when I hadn't got anything.
One morning I set the lathe speed wrong because I was too scared to check. A whole batch of parts was ruined. I thought I'd be sent home.
Instead the foreman, old Joshi-ji, sat me down with a cup of tea and said, "Show me what you think you're doing." I showed him. He didn't laugh once. In one hour with him I learned more than in three months with Bhosale.
It wasn't that the lathe was hard, beta. It was that I was afraid to ask.

For my first year as a café manager, I trained people by asking, "Got it?" They always said yes. Then they closed the till wrong.
Last month, Anjali joined. Before I showed her anything, I asked what she already knew. She had worked in her uncle's shop, counting cash at night. So I said, "Closing the till is your uncle's shop, plus one screen."
I showed her one full close, slowly. Then, instead of "Got it?", I said, "Tell me the steps back, your way." She got four out of five. She'd missed printing the summary. We fixed that.
Then I gave her a small task: close the morning till while I watched and didn't speak. She did it with only one pause.
I'm Jeevan, and I used to think nodding meant understanding. It mostly means someone is being polite. Now I only trust what I've seen someone do.

Team lead's note, customer support floor, Thursday.
I watched Uma train our new hire, Parul, on the refund process today, and I want to record it.
Uma began by asking Parul what she already knew. Parul had returned things online herself, so Uma said, "Good, you've been the customer. Now you're the other side."

Uma didn't correct her immediately; she asked, "What if the order is three months old?" Parul thought and found the gap herself.

Most trainers ask, "Any doubts?" and accept silence. I will ask Uma to show the others this method next week.
— Team lead, Support

The car jerked forward and stalled. Then again. Priscila slapped the wheel. Ivan, who had learned to drive with his own father shouting, waited for the shouting to begin.
